Thought: I need to determine what happens when organic phosphates, phosphothioates or phosphodithioates are mixed with non-oxidizing acids. This is a chemistry safety question about potential chemical reactions.

Organic phosphates, phosphothioates, and phosphodithioates are organophosphorus compounds commonly found in pesticides and other agricultural chemicals. When these compounds react with acids, they can undergo hydrolysis reactions.

The key concern with many organophosphorus compounds is that when they decompose (such as through acid hydrolysis), they can release toxic gases - particularly phosphine (PH₃) or hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) in the case of the sulfur-containing variants (phosphothioates and phosphodithioates).

These gases are highly toxic even in small amounts. Hydrogen sulfide has a characteristic rotten egg smell and is toxic to the respiratory system. Phosphine is extremely toxic and can cause severe respiratory issues, among other health problems.

Therefore, the main safety risk when mixing these organophosphorus compounds with non-oxidizing acids would be the generation of toxic gases.

Looking at the options, H (Toxic gas generation) appears to be the correct answer.
